title: Multi-Region & Disaster Recovery
subtitle: Lose an entire region on purpose, and see how much data and time each recovery design costs you.
learn: What RPO and RTO mean and how they drive design and cost
Why replicas are not backups, and what each one protects against
Active-passive versus active-active regions and their trade-offs
How data residency rules limit where data may be copied
Why untested failover plans tend to fail, and how drills fix that

steps.title: A whole region goes dark
steps.body: Your shop runs in region A, a cluster of data centers in one metro area. Today a power and networking failure takes the entire region offline. Not one server: everything, including the database. Multi-region design is the plan for that day. Two questions decide it: how much recent data can you afford to lose, and how long can you afford to be down?
steps.idea: Disaster recovery starts with two business questions, not with technology.
steps.caption: All traffic flows to region A today.

steps.title: RPO and RTO
steps.body: RPO, the recovery point objective, is how much data you can lose, measured as time: an RPO of 5 minutes means the newest 5 minutes of writes may vanish. RTO, the recovery time objective, is how long the service may stay down. Both are targets the business picks. Tighter targets cost more, so a payments ledger and a recommendations cache should not share the same numbers.
steps.idea: RPO is data lost, RTO is time lost; each step toward zero costs roughly an order of magnitude more.
steps.caption: Two clocks start ticking when the region fails.

steps.title: A standby copy in region B
steps.body: Region B keeps a replica of the database. Writes commit in region A, then stream to B asynchronously, because waiting for a cross-region acknowledgment on every write would add roughly 60 to 150 ms. The cost is replication lag, typically under a second but spiking under load. Anything not yet shipped when A dies is lost, so lag is your real RPO.
steps.idea: Asynchronous replication is fast but its lag is exactly the data you can lose.
steps.caption: Writes stream to B about one second behind.

steps.title: A replica is not a backup
steps.body: A replica copies every change, including your mistakes. If a bad deploy runs DELETE without a WHERE clause, the replica faithfully deletes the same rows a moment later. Backups are point-in-time copies kept separately, often in another region or account, with logs so you can restore to just before the mistake. Replicas fight hardware loss; backups fight human error, corruption, and ransomware.
steps.idea: Replicas give availability; backups give history. You need both.
steps.caption: The bad write replicates, but the vault keeps history.

steps.title: Region A fails
steps.body: Region A is now unreachable. The router's health checks fail, and requests to region A time out. The replica in B holds everything up to about one second ago, so roughly that much data is stranded in A. If you promote B automatically while A is only partitioned, not dead, both sides might accept writes: the split-brain problem, so many teams require a human to confirm.
steps.idea: The failure itself is easy to see; deciding that it is real is the hard part.
steps.caption: Region A stops answering; B has a copy.

steps.title: Active-passive failover
steps.body: In active-passive, B is a warm standby. An engineer promotes the replica to primary, scales up the app tier, and flips the router so users go to B. With a rehearsed runbook and a warm standby this commonly takes 5 to 30 minutes, a cold standby takes hours. The outcome here: RPO of about 1 second, RTO of about 10 minutes.
steps.idea: Active-passive is cheaper and simpler, but you pay in minutes of downtime and an idle region.
steps.caption: Traffic shifts to B after the replica is promoted.

steps.title: Active-active
steps.body: In active-active, both regions serve users all the time, so losing one just means the router sends everyone to the other, which must already have spare capacity, about 2x headroom for two regions. RTO drops to seconds. The price is write conflicts: two regions can change the same record at once, so you need conflict rules, per-user home regions, or a globally consistent database that pays cross-region latency on commits.
steps.idea: Active-active buys near-zero RTO at the cost of conflict handling, double capacity, and complexity.
steps.caption: Both regions serve traffic and replicate each way.

steps.title: Data residency
steps.body: Laws such as the GDPR and national data-localization rules can require that some users' data stay in a specific country or bloc. That conflicts with the casual idea of copying everything to the other region. Teams usually pin each user to a home region and replicate only to approved partner regions, keeping backups in-jurisdiction too. Residency may force a cheaper, slower recovery design for that data. Confirm the rules with legal counsel.
steps.idea: Where recovery data may live is a legal constraint, so check it before choosing the failover region.
steps.caption: EU users' data stays in EU regions only.

steps.title: Failover drills
steps.body: A plan nobody has run is a guess. Real failures expose stale credentials, missing capacity in region B, DNS caches that ignore your short TTL, and runbooks that depend on a tool living in the dead region. Teams run drills: shift a small share of traffic, then a full game day that fails over for real, and measure actual RPO and RTO against the targets. Fail back, too, since going home is its own migration.
steps.idea: Only a measured drill tells you your real RTO; practice turns a guess into a number.
steps.caption: A drill shifts traffic to B and measures the clock.

steps.title: Pick the cheapest design that meets the targets
steps.body: Set RPO and RTO per system from the cost of downtime and data loss. Use replicas for fast failover and backups for history, because they solve different problems. Active-passive is simpler and slower, active-active is faster and harder. Check data residency before copying data anywhere, and drill regularly so the numbers on paper are the numbers you actually get.
steps.idea: Replicas for speed, backups for history, drills for truth.
steps.caption: Targets, copies, and drills together form the plan.

quiz.q: A team's database replica lags the primary by about 2 seconds under normal load. The region fails and they promote the replica. Roughly what is their data loss?
options: None, because the replica has a full copy
About 2 seconds of recent writes
About 24 hours, the backup interval
Only writes from the failed region's cache
quiz.why: Asynchronous replicas trail the primary by the lag, so writes in that window never left the failed region. Lag is effectively your RPO.

quiz.q: A buggy migration deletes a customer table at 14:02. Why does the cross-region replica not save you?
options: Replicas only store indexes, not rows
Replication copies the delete to the replica within moments
Replicas are read-only so they cannot be restored
Cross-region replication is too slow to matter
quiz.why: Replication is faithful, including mistakes. You need point-in-time backups with logs to restore to 14:01.

quiz.q: The business says the service may be down at most 30 seconds in a region loss. Which design fits best?
options: Nightly backups copied to another region
A cold standby rebuilt from infrastructure code
Active-passive with a manual runbook
Active-active with enough spare capacity in each region
quiz.why: Only a design where the other region is already serving traffic reaches RTO in seconds. Manual promotion typically takes minutes or more.

quiz.q: You add active-active writes in two regions. What new problem must you solve that active-passive avoided?
options: Backups become impossible
Two regions may update the same record concurrently, creating conflicts
DNS can no longer route users
Replication lag becomes zero
quiz.why: With a single writer there is one order of changes. With two writers you need conflict rules, home-region ownership, or a globally consistent store.

quiz.q: A runbook has never been executed. What is the most likely outcome in a real region failure?
options: It works, since the steps are written down
Actual recovery takes longer than the stated RTO because of hidden gaps
The replica fixes itself
Failover is skipped and traffic stays in the failed region by design
quiz.why: Untested plans hide expired credentials, capacity shortfalls, and dependencies on the failed region. Drills reveal them before they cost you.

cheatsheet.def: Recovery point objective: the most data, measured in time, you accept losing. Set by lag or backup interval.
Recovery time objective: the longest acceptable outage from failure until service is restored.
Replicas copy changes live for fast failover, mistakes included. Backups are separate point-in-time history for restoring.
One region serves traffic; another stands by. Simpler and cheaper, RTO in minutes to hours.
Several regions serve traffic at once. RTO in seconds, but needs spare capacity and conflict handling.
Two regions both believe they are primary and accept conflicting writes. Prevent with fencing or human confirmation.
Legal rules limiting where data and its copies may be stored. It constrains replica and backup placement.
A planned drill that fails over for real and measures actual RPO and RTO against targets.
